summary.text: Lucas-type binomial congruences pair the terms indexed by \(k\) and \(p+k\) with opposite signs, giving \(a(p+r)\equiv c(p+r)\equiv0\pmod p\) for \(0\le r<p\); they also give \(a(p-1)\equiv1\) and show that only the middle term survives in \(c(p-1)\), yielding \(c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\). Reversing the columns of each Hankel matrix then makes it triangular with this constant diagonal, and the reversal sign \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\) gives the two claimed determinant residues.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                    \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and put
\[
m=\frac{p-1}{2},
\qquad\text{so that}\qquad p=2m+1.
\]
All congruences in the proof are modulo \(p\).

We will first establish the binomial-coefficient congruences needed for the two sequences, then prove the required vanishing and endpoint evaluations, and finally evaluate the determinants.

### 1. Binomial congruences

We repeatedly use the following two-digit form of Lucas's congruence. If
\[
N=N_0+pN_1,\qquad K=K_0+pK_1,
\qquad 0\leq N_0,K_0<p,
\]
then
\[
\binom NK\equiv \binom{N_0}{K_0}\binom{N_1}{K_1}\pmod p.
\]
This follows by comparing coefficients in
\[
(1+X)^N=(1+X)^{N_0}\bigl((1+X)^p\bigr)^{N_1}
       \equiv(1+X)^{N_0}(1+X^p)^{N_1}\pmod p,
\]
since every intermediate binomial coefficient \(\binom pj\), \(0<j<p\), is divisible by \(p\). The same argument with more base-\(p\) digits gives the usual general form, though only the small cases below are needed.

First, for \(0\leq k<p\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, this is immediate from
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}
 =\frac{(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)}{k!}
 \equiv\frac{(-1)(-2)\cdots(-k)}{k!}=(-1)^k.
\]
(The denominator is invertible modulo \(p\) because \(k<p\).)

Next let \(0\leq r<p\) and \(0\leq k\leq p+r\). Lucas's congruence gives
\[
\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv
\begin{cases}
\binom rk,&0\leq k<p,\\[4pt]
\binom r{k-p},&p\leq k\leq p+r.
\end{cases} \tag{2}
\]
For in the first case the base-\(p\) digits of \(k\) are \((k,0)\), while in the second they are \((k-p,1)\); the digits of \(p+r\) are \((r,1)\).

We also need central binomial coefficients. Write
\[
B_s=\binom{2s}{s},\qquad D_s=\binom{2(p+s)}{p+s}
\]
for \(0\leq s<p\). There are two cases.

If \(2s<p\), then there is no carry in doubling \(s\), and Lucas gives
\[
D_s\equiv \binom{2s}{s}\binom 21=2B_s. \tag{3}
\]
If \(2s\geq p\), then the base-\(p\) units digit of \(2s\) is \(2s-p<s\). Hence Lucas gives
\[
B_s=\binom{2s}{s}\equiv \binom{2s-p}{s}\binom10=0. \tag{4}
\]
Likewise, \(2(p+s)=3p+(2s-p)\), whereas \(p+s\) has digits \((s,1)\), so
\[
D_s\equiv \binom{2s-p}{s}\binom31=0. \tag{5}
\]
Thus in fact (3), namely
\[
D_s\equiv2B_s, \tag{6}
\]
holds for every \(0\leq s<p\): in the carry case both sides vanish.

A consequence that will pair the central factors in the definition of \(c\) is that, for any \(0\leq x,s<p\),
\[
B_xD_s\equiv D_xB_s. \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, if both \(2x<p\) and \(2s<p\), then each side is \(2B_xB_s\). If at least one of these inequalities fails, the corresponding small central coefficient and its shifted counterpart both vanish by (4)--(5), so both sides are again equal. Equivalently, (7) follows immediately from (6).

### 2. Vanishing of \(a(p+r)\)

We claim that for every \(r\) with \(0\leq r<p\),
\[
a(p+r)\equiv0. \tag{8}
\]
Split its defining sum into the terms with \(0\leq k<p\) and those with \(k=p+x\), \(0\leq x\leq r\). By (2), for \(k<p\),
\[
(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^4
 \equiv(-1)^k\binom rk^4.
\]
When \(k>r\), the right side is zero. Thus the lower part of the sum equals
\[
S=\sum_{x=0}^r(-1)^x\binom rx^4.
\]
For the upper part, (2) and the oddness of \(p\) give
\[
(-1)^{p+x}\binom{p+r}{p+x}^4
 \equiv-(-1)^x\binom rx^4.
\]
Consequently the upper part is \(-S\), proving (8).

### 3. The value of \(a(p-1)\)

By (1),
\[
a(p-1)
 \equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4
 =\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\]
There are an odd number \(p=2m+1\) of terms, so the alternating sum is \(1\). Hence
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1. \tag{9}
\]

### 4. Vanishing of \(c(p+r)\)

We next claim that for every \(0\leq r<p\),
\[
c(p+r)\equiv0. \tag{10}
\]
Again split the sum at \(p\). For \(0\leq x<p\), formula (2) gives
\[
\binom{p+r}{x}\equiv\binom rx.
\]
If \(x>r\), this is zero. If \(0\leq x\leq r\), put \(s=r-x\). Then
\[
p+r-x=p+s,
\]
so the term indexed by \(x\) in the lower part is congruent to
\[
L_x=(-1)^x\binom rx^2 B_xD_s. \tag{11}
\]

The corresponding term in the upper part has index \(p+x\). Since
\[
(p+r)-(p+x)=r-x=s,
\]
formula (2) gives
\[
\binom{p+r}{p+x}\equiv\binom rx.
\]
Its two central factors are \(D_x\) and \(B_s\), and because \(p\) is odd, \((-1)^{p+x}=-(-1)^x\). Therefore this upper term is congruent to
\[
U_x=-(-1)^x\binom rx^2D_xB_s. \tag{12}
\]
By the central-factor identity (7), \(B_xD_s\equiv D_xB_s\), and hence \(U_x\equiv-L_x\). Every lower term with \(x>r\) vanishes, while the lower terms with \(0\leq x\leq r\) cancel one-for-one with all the upper terms. This proves (10).

For completeness, the central-factor equality used here incorporates all four carry possibilities: neither \(2x\) nor \(2s\) reaches \(p\), exactly one does, or both do. In the no-carry case both products equal \(2B_xB_s\); in each remaining case a factor on each side is zero. Thus no exceptional value of \(x\) or \(s=r-x\) is omitted.

### 5. The value of \(c(p-1)\)

Now \(p-1=2m\). Consider the summand of \(c(2m)\) indexed by \(k\), where \(0\leq k\leq2m<p\).

If \(k<m\), then \(2m-k>m\), so
\[
2(2m-k)\geq2m+2>2m+1=p.
\]
Since \(2m-k<p\), the carry case (4) applies and gives
\[
\binom{2(2m-k)}{2m-k}\equiv0.
\]
Thus every term with \(k<m\) vanishes.

If \(k>m\), then \(2k\geq2m+2>p\), while \(k<p\), so (4) gives
\[
\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0.
\]
Thus every term with \(k>m\) also vanishes. Only the middle term \(k=m\) remains.

Let
\[
Q=\binom{2m}{m}=\binom{p-1}{m}.
\]
By (1), \(Q\equiv(-1)^m\). The middle term contains \(Q^2\) from \(\binom{2m}{m}^2\), and one further copy of \(Q\) from each of the two central factors. Therefore
\[
c(p-1)=c(2m)\equiv(-1)^mQ^4=(-1)^m, \tag{13}
\]
because \(Q^2\equiv1\).

### 6. A sparse Hankel determinant lemma

We now record the determinant argument common to both sequences. Let \(s(0),s(1),\ldots\) be any sequence modulo \(p=2m+1\), and suppose
\[
s(p+r)=0\quad(0\leq r<p),
\qquad s(p-1)=t. \tag{14}
\]
Form the \(p\times p\) Hankel matrix
\[
M=(s(i+j))_{0\leq i,j<p}.
\]
Reverse the order of its columns. The resulting matrix \(B\) has entries
\[
B_{ij}=s\bigl(i+(p-1-j)\bigr).
\]
If \(i>j\), then
\[
i+(p-1-j)=p+(i-j-1),
\]
and \(0\leq i-j-1<p\). By (14), \(B_{ij}=0\). Thus \(B\) is upper triangular. Its diagonal entries are
\[
B_{ii}=s(i+p-1-i)=s(p-1)=t,
\]
so
\[
\det B=t^p. \tag{15}
\]

The reversal of \(p\) columns has \(p(p-1)/2\) inversions, hence sign
\[
(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}.
\]
Since \(p=2m+1\),
\[
\frac{p(p-1)}2=pm,
\]
and \(p\) is odd, so this sign is \((-1)^m\). Column reversal therefore gives
\[
\det B=(-1)^m\det M. \tag{16}
\]
Combining (15) and (16), and noting that \((-1)^m\) is its own inverse, yields
\[
\det M=(-1)^m t^p. \tag{17}
\]

### 7. Application to the two matrices

Let
\[
A=(a(i+j))_{0\leq i,j<p}.
\]
By (8), its defining sequence satisfies \(a(p+r)\equiv0\) for \(0\leq r<p\), and by (9), \(a(p-1)\equiv1\). Applying (17) with \(t=1\) gives
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^m=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.
\]

Similarly, let
\[
C=(c(i+j))_{0\leq i,j<p}.
\]
By (10), \(c(p+r)\equiv0\) for \(0\leq r<p\), and by (13), \(c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m\). Formula (17) now gives
\[
\det C\equiv(-1)^m\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p.
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p=(-1)^m\). Hence
\[
\det C\equiv(-1)^{2m}=1\pmod p.
\]

Finally, reducing an integer matrix entrywise modulo \(p\) commutes with taking its determinant, because the determinant is an integer polynomial in the matrix entries. Thus the determinant computations above are exactly the asserted integer congruences. Therefore, for every odd prime \(p\),
\[
\boxed{\det(a(i+j))_{0\leq i,j<p}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\det(c(i+j))_{0\leq i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p}.
\]
